output.statement: For nonzero integers a,b,c,d with a+b+c+d=0, let N1>=N2>=N3>=N4 be the rearranged magnitudes and A0=|a*b|,B0=|c*d|. Then N1<=3*N2, (1/|d|)min(A0/B0,B0/A0)<=3/N3 and |a+b|/max(A0,B0)<=6/N3. Moreover for any nonnegative x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4 in ell^2(Z\{0}), sum_(a+b+c+d=0,abcd!=0) product_(j=1)^4 x_j(k_j)/N3(a,b,c,d)<=C*product_j||x_j||_(ell^2), where (k_1,k_2,k_3,k_4)=(a,b,c,d), and C is absolute. The same bound holds on any subset of these interactions, and the infinite positive sum is the supremum of its finite restrictions.

argument.text: For the pointwise assertions fix integers a,b,c,d and assume L1: abcd!=0 and a+b+c+d=0. Order their magnitudes as N1>=N2>=N3>=N4. The largest is bounded by the sum of the other three, so N1<=3*N2. Put A0=|ab|, B0=|cd|. If d is among the two largest, min(A0/B0,B0/A0)<=1 and 1/|d|<=1/N3. If not, the largest two are among a,b,c. If they are a,b, use B0/A0 to bound the desired expression by |c|/|ab|<=1/N3. If they are a,c, their ratio lies in [1/3,3]. Therefore the expression is at most 3*min(|b|/|d|^2,1/|b|)<=3/max(|b|,|d|)=3/N3: use the first alternative if |d|>=|b| and the second otherwise. The case b,c is identical after swapping a,b. This proves the first majorant.

For the second majorant, if the two largest are in the same pair of (a,b),(c,d), the other pair sums to magnitude at most 2*N3. Since a+b=-(c+d), |a+b|/max(A0,B0)<=2*N3/(N1*N2)<=2/N3. If they lie in different pairs, the third largest is paired with one of them, whence max(A0,B0)>=N2*N3; also |a+b|<=2*N1<=6*N2 by F001. The quotient is <=6/N3. Any ordering of ties is covered. Discharge L1; these are the claimed conditional pointwise statements for all such frequencies.

Fix four nonnegative ell^2 sequences x_r. First restrict all of them to finitely many frequencies. Decompose each into shells 2^j<=|k|<2^(j+1), j>=0, and let Xshell_(r,j) be its ell^2 norm there. Fix one of the at most 24 orderings of the four shell indices j1>=j2>=j3>=j4, permuting the sequence labels accordingly. A nonzero zero-sum interaction requires j1-j2<=2, since otherwise the largest magnitude would exceed the sum of the other three. For each fixed pair of the two smaller frequencies, sum the two larger-frequency sequences subject to their prescribed sum. Cauchy-Schwarz, applied to a translated reflection, bounds that sum by their shell ell^2 norm product. A shell contains at most 2^(j+1) integers, so summing each smaller sequence in ell^1 costs at most C*2^(j/2) times its ell^2 norm. Thus the shell contribution without the weight is <=C*2^((j3+j4)/2)*product_r Xshell_(r,jr). On that shell N3>=2^j3, so the weight leaves C*2^(-(j3-j4)/2).

produces.statement: For every ordered four-shell zero-sum interaction j1>=j2>=j3>=j4, its weighted contribution is <=C*2^(-(j3-j4)/2)*product_r Xshell_(r,jr), and j1-j2 is in {0,1,2}.

argument.text: For each q in {0,1,2}, set j1=J,j2=J-q. Drop the upper restrictions on the smaller shells; nonnegativity increases the sum. F002 bounds the ordered contribution by C*(sum_J Xshell_(1,J)*Xshell_(2,J-q))*(sum_(ell>=m>=0)2^(-(ell-m)/2)*Xshell_(3,ell)*Xshell_(4,m)). The first factor is at most ||Xshell_1||_ell2||Xshell_2||_ell2. Set r=ell-m; for each r the second correlation is at most ||Xshell_3||_ell2||Xshell_4||_ell2 by Cauchy-Schwarz, so the second factor is at most sum_(r>=0)2^(-r/2)||Xshell_3||_ell2||Xshell_4||_ell2=||Xshell_3||_ell2||Xshell_4||_ell2/(1-2^(-1/2)). Shell disjointness identifies each shell-norm ell^2 norm with ||x_r||_ell2. Sum over 24 orderings and three offsets. This proves the finite bound with an absolute constant.

argument.text: For arbitrary nonnegative ell^2 sequences restrict all inputs to |k|<=m and apply F003. Their norms are bounded by the full norms. Every finite subset of interactions is included in some such restriction, so the infinite positive sum, defined as the supremum over finite subsums, has the same bound. Restricting to any subset only decreases that nonnegative sum. Together with the pointwise assertions this proves the output assertion without exchanging conditionally convergent sums.
